explanation: The pole fires on the predicate vocabulary of technical and scientific exposition: past participles and relational adjectives that state what was done to, or what holds of, a subject (treated, monitored, measured, sequenced, collected, extracted, exposed, affected; resistant, compatible, amenable, feasible, valid, applicable, susceptible, attributable, liable, worth, able), plus the causal, cessative and preventive verbs such prose uses (cause/causes/caused/causing, prevent/prevented/preventing, cure(d), treat(ed/ing), halt(ed), reduce(d), stop(ped)); the class is the predicate, not the individual trigger word, so it generalises to unseen members of it. It peaks on such a predicate in a relative or that-clause claim about an inanimate or biological subject ('the virus that causes', 'the cells were treated', 'the study shows that the drug stopped'), and stays near its floor (about -0.17) on words that name entities in any topic (dog, patient, celebrity, hierarchy, theory), on physical-property adjectives (viscous, acidic, elastic) and on narrative or everyday verbs (walked, talked, played, made, started, ended).
